204.title: The body is the field
204.hook: the Gita began on a battlefield; chapter thirteen says the real field is you
204.carry: the body is the field; you're its knower
204.howItsDone: Hindu teachers often use Gita 13's field and knower of the field (kshetra and kshetrajna) in meditation and study, as a way of noticing the body and mind as something known, and asking who the knower is.

segments.voice: Yesterday, priya: the one dear to me, a portrait of the devoted person. Your line was free from hate, friendly to all. Today, a new chapter, and a new picture.

Go back to the Gita's very first line. The blind king Dhritarashtra asks: on the field of dharma, the field of the Kurus, what did my sons and the sons of Pandu do? Dharmakshetre, kurukshetre. The whole book opens on a field. Two armies, dust, chariots, a man about to break down. Twelve chapters later, chapter thirteen picks up that same word, field, kshetra, and turns it around. The field, Krishna says, isn't only out there where the armies stand. You're standing in it. You are it.
screen: `ON THE FIELD OF DHARMA.` → `TWO ARMIES, ONE FIELD.` → `THE FIELD IS YOU.`

segments.voice: Chapter thirteen opens with a definition. This body, Arjuna, is called the field, and the one who knows it, the sages call the knower of the field. Kshetra, the field. Kshetrajna, the knower of the field. Picture a farmer's field. Weeds and wheat grow there. Weather passes over it. Seasons change it. And at the edge stands someone who watches it and knows it, who isn't the dirt. Hindu teachers call that knower in you the atman, the self. Then the line that makes this chapter famous: know me also as the knower of the field in all fields. The same knower, in every body. Hindu schools read that line differently. Advaita teachers say the knower in you and the divine knower are finally one. Ramanuja and the Vaishnava schools say the divine dwells in every knower as its inner guide, close but not identical. Both read it from the same verse. Then verses five and six list what's in the field, and the list is bigger than you'd guess. The elements. The sense of I. The intellect. The senses and the mind, and what they reach for. Desire, aversion, pleasure, pain, the body as a whole, awareness, steadiness. Your wanting, your not wanting, even your moods: all field, things that grow and change and pass. So when anger comes up, the Gita's picture says: something is growing in the field. You can notice it from the edge. You are not only the weather.
screen: `THIS BODY IS CALLED THE FIELD.` · `THE KNOWER OF THE FIELD.` · `THE KNOWER IN ALL FIELDS.` · `EVEN DESIRE AND PAIN ARE FIELD.` · then, large: `THE BODY IS THE FIELD.`

segments.voice: Walk the edge of your own field: the body's weight, its warmth, the places that ache; the breath coming and going; a thought arriving, maybe a worry, maybe a wish. Field, all of it. Then, for a moment, notice the one noticing, without naming it, and just watch things grow and pass from the edge.
Kshetra, the field. Gita thirteen: the body, with its senses, desires and moods, is the field; the one who knows it is the knower of the field, kshetrajna.
Your line: the body is the field; you're its knower. The same word the Gita opens with, turned inward. More of the field tomorrow.

205.title: Knowledge starts with humility
205.hook: Arjuna argues like an expert, then says: teach me. The Gita's list of knowledge starts there.
205.tomorrow: The same Lord in all beings
205.howItsDone: Hindu teachers often quote Gita 13.7–13.11 as a checklist of character for students, starting with amanitva, humility; many traditions treat serving and honoring the teacher as part of this knowledge.

segments.voice: Yesterday, kshetra: the body is the field; you're its knower. Today, what the knower actually knows.
screen: `KSHETRA: THE BODY IS THE FIELD; YOU'RE ITS KNOWER.`

segments.voice: At the start of the Gita, Arjuna argues like an expert. He's a great archer and a prince, and he lays out the case against this war: family will be destroyed, the old ways will fall, it's wrong to kill your own teachers. Then, a few verses into chapter two, he stops. He admits his mind is confused about what's right. And he says to Krishna: I am your student. I've taken refuge in you. Teach me. That's the moment the Gita really begins. Not when Arjuna knows the most, but when he admits he doesn't.
screen: `ARJUNA ARGUES LIKE AN EXPERT.` → `THEN: I AM YOUR STUDENT.` → `TEACH ME.`

segments.voice: Chapter thirteen turns that moment into a list. Verse seven. Krishna gives a heading, knowledge, and the first word under it is amanitva: humility, not thinking much of yourself. Then adambhitva, no pretending. Then ahimsa, doing no harm. Then patience, straightforwardness, serving your teacher, cleanliness, steadiness, self-control. In many Hindu homes that line still lives in the body: you bow, or touch an elder's feet, before you learn from them. The list keeps going. Not being dragged by the senses. Not being ruled by the sense of I. Not clinging too tightly to home and family. Staying even when things go well and when they don't. Steady devotion. A taste for quiet places. Then the surprise. This, Krishna says, is called knowledge, and whatever is its opposite is ajnana, ignorance. So in the Gita, knowledge isn't only what's in your head; it's how you live. A brilliant, arrogant person, by this definition, is missing the first item. From verse twelve the chapter turns to what is to be known, Brahman, and the words go strange on purpose. It has hands and feet everywhere, eyes and faces everywhere. It's far away, and it's near, inside beings and outside them. Verse seventeen calls it the light of lights, beyond darkness. And the door to it starts where Arjuna started: humility.
screen: `FIRST ON THE LIST: HUMILITY.` · `BOW BEFORE YOU LEARN.` · `THE OPPOSITE IS IGNORANCE.` · `KNOWLEDGE IS HOW YOU LIVE.` · then, large: `KNOWLEDGE STARTS WITH HUMILITY.`

segments.voice: Think of a recent moment you needed to be right, a text thread, a meeting, a family dinner, and just see it. Replay it with the need dropped one notch: ask a question instead of making a point. Then do what Arjuna did. If you pray, bow your head and ask God, teach me. If you don't, say it inwardly to the day ahead: i don't know everything yet. Notice how that softer version feels in the chest.
Amanitva, humility, not thinking much of yourself. Gita thirteen, seven: the first word on the list Krishna calls knowledge; its opposite is ignorance.
Your line: amanitva: knowledge begins with humility. Arjuna's did: teach me. Day two hundred five, done.

206.title: The same Lord in all beings
206.hook: an outcaste in a narrow lane asks Shankara a question; chapter thirteen gives the same answer with one sun
206.carry: the same Lord lives in every being
206.howItsDone: Many Hindus greet others with namaste, often explained as honoring the divine in the other person; Gita 13.27–13.28, seeing the same Lord in all beings, is one of the verses teachers point to for this.

segments.voice: Yesterday: amanitva: knowledge begins with humility, first on the Gita's list. Today, the chapter's last and biggest picture.

There's a story told about Shankara, the great teacher of oneness. In Kashi, coming up from the Ganga, he meets an outcaste man with his dogs in a narrow lane, and Shankara, or in some tellings his students, calls out: move aside. The man doesn't. He asks: move what? This body made of food, away from that one? Or the self, away from the self? Is the sun shining in the Ganga a different sun from the one in the water of my lane? Tradition says Shankara bowed to him and called him his teacher. Chapter thirteen ends on the same picture.
screen: `MOVE ASIDE.` → `MOVE WHAT? THE SELF FROM THE SELF?` → `ONE SUN IN EVERY WATER.`

segments.voice: First, two words. Prakriti: nature, everything that moves and changes, the body, the senses, the mind. Purusha: the person, the conscious one who experiences it. Verse twenty: nature is behind all doing; the person is behind the experiencing of pleasure and pain. Then verse twenty-seven, the center of today. The one who sees the supreme Lord standing the same in all beings, not perishing when they perish, truly sees. Verse twenty-eight follows: samam pashyan, seeing the same Lord everywhere, such a person doesn't harm the self by the self. Commentators unpack that line in more than one way. Some readers hear in it: if the same one lives in everyone, hurting another is hurting yourself. Verse twenty-nine: the one who sees that nature does the acting, and that the self is not the doer, sees. Near the end come two pictures. Verse thirty-two: space is everywhere, and it's so subtle it's never stained by what it holds. So the self in every body is never stained. Verse thirty-three: as the one sun lights this whole world, the knower of the field lights the whole field. One light, many fields. The schools differ again on how literally to take the oneness: Advaita as one self, Vaishnava schools as one Lord dwelling in many selves. Either way, the verse asks for the seeing the man in the lane asked of Shankara: look at anyone, and see the same Lord.
screen: `NATURE ACTS. THE PERSON KNOWS.` · `SEEING THE SAME LORD EVERYWHERE.` · `HARM NONE, HARM NOT YOURSELF.` · `NEVER STAINED. ONE SUN, MANY FIELDS.` · then, large: `THE SAME LORD IN ALL BEINGS.`

segments.voice: Picture a light at your center, steady and warm, then the same light in the person nearest you, in the next room or the next house. Widen it: someone across town, someone whose name you'll never know, and, if you're willing, someone you find hard. Greet each one inwardly with namaste, i bow to you. If you pray, add: the same Lord lives in you. If you don't, simply see the same light. You don't have to like them; just see it.
Sama, the same, even. Gita thirteen, twenty-seven: the one who sees the same Lord standing in all beings, imperishable in the perishing, truly sees.
Your line: the same Lord lives in every being. One sun, in every water. See you tomorrow.

207.title: The three gunas
207.hook: Arjuna once asked what pushes us to do wrong; chapter fourteen names the three threads woven through everything
207.carry: nature is woven of three gunas
207.howItsDone: The three gunas are part of Hindu vocabulary: some people describe foods, habits, music and moods as sattvic, rajasic or tamasic, and Ayurveda and yoga teachers use the terms too.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the same Lord lives in every being, one sun on every field. Today, what the field itself is woven from.

Back in chapter three, Arjuna asked Krishna a question almost everyone has asked. What pushes a person to do wrong, even when they don't want to, as if by force? Krishna's answer was short: it's desire, it's anger, born of rajas. Arjuna didn't get the whole map then. Eleven chapters later, he does. Chapter fourteen names the three forces Hindu thought sees in everything in nature: in food, in music, in mornings and moods, and in Arjuna too.
screen: `WHAT PUSHES US TO DO WRONG?` → `BORN OF RAJAS.` → `THE WHOLE MAP: THREE THREADS.`

segments.voice: Verse five. Sattva, rajas, tamas: these gunas, born of nature, bind the undying one in the body. Guna means a quality, and in ordinary Sanskrit it can also mean a strand or a thread, even the cord of a bowstring. So picture a rope of three strands twisted together. Everything in nature is all three, in different mixes. Sattva is clarity, brightness, balance. Verse six: it's clear, it lights things up, it's free of trouble. But even sattva binds, by attachment to happiness and to knowledge. You can get hooked on feeling good and feeling wise. Rajas is passion, motion, heat. Verse seven: it comes from craving and attachment, and binds by attachment to action. It's the part of you that can't stop doing. Tamas is darkness, heaviness, inertia. Verse eight: born of ignorance, it deludes, and binds through carelessness, laziness and sleep. Verse nine sums up: sattva ties you to happiness, rajas to action, and tamas covers understanding and ties you to heedlessness. So none of the three is simply the good one. Even the bright thread is still a thread. And some teachers stress that this is a description, not a verdict: rest needs a little tamas, and getting out of bed needs a little rajas. The point isn't to hate any strand. It's to see the rope. Our word is the first and clearest of the three: sattva.
screen: `GUNA: A QUALITY, A THREAD.` · `SATTVA: CLEAR AND BRIGHT.` · `RAJAS: PASSION AND MOTION.` · `TAMAS: HEAVY AND DARK.` · then, large: `SATTVA.`

segments.voice: Check your own rope right now: heaviness or a pull toward blankness is the dark thread; buzzing, a list running, is the moving thread; any clarity, even a moment of simply seeing, is the bright one. Don't pick a favorite; just notice the mix. At your next meal, look at the plate the way Gita seventeen sorts food: fresh and nourishing is sattva; very sharp, salty or burning is rajas; stale and leftover is tamas.
Sattva. Clarity, brightness, balance: the first of the three gunas, the strands of nature, with rajas, motion, and tamas, heaviness.
Your line: nature is woven of three gunas. Clarity, motion, heaviness, twisted into one rope. That's day two hundred seven.

208.title: The three robbers
208.hook: Ramakrishna's three robbers in a forest, and the Gita's field marks for each guna
208.carry: tamas strikes, rajas binds, sattva shows the road
208.howItsDone: Some Hindus use the gunas as a practical check on daily life, choosing food, company and routines that support sattva; some teachers use Gita 14.11–14.13 to describe what each guna looks like.

segments.voice: Yesterday: nature is woven of three gunas, sattva, rajas and tamas, twisted like one rope. Today, how to spot each one, and a story about where they leave you.

Ramakrishna, the nineteenth-century saint of Bengal, told this one. A traveler is crossing a forest when three robbers jump him and take everything. The first says: why keep him alive? and reaches for his knife. The second says: no, just tie him up. They tie him and walk off. Later the third comes back alone, unties him, says sorry, and walks him to the main road. That's your way home, he says. Come with me, the traveler begs. I can't, says the robber. The police would know me. The forest, Ramakrishna said, is this world. The three robbers are the gunas.
screen: `ONE REACHES FOR A KNIFE.` → `ONE TIES HIM UP.` → `ONE SHOWS HIM THE ROAD.`

segments.voice: In the Gita, Krishna gives Arjuna the field marks of the same three. Verse ten: one thread rises by pushing down the other two, so the mix is always shifting. Verse eleven: when light and understanding shine through every gate of the body, the eyes, the ears, the mind, sattva is strong. Verse twelve: greed, busyness, starting one project after another, restlessness, longing: that's rajas rising. Verse thirteen: darkness, sluggishness, carelessness, confusion: that's tamas. Verse seventeen follows each to where it leads: from sattva, knowledge; from rajas, greed; from tamas, confusion. Verse eighteen gives a direction: those in sattva rise, those in rajas stay in the middle, those in tamas sink. The chapter even says the thread you're in at the end of life shapes what comes next. Then verse nineteen: when the seer sees no doer other than the gunas, and knows what is beyond them, that one reaches my being. That's how Ramakrishna read the robbers. Tamas would destroy you, rajas ties you up, sattva unties you and points to the road, but even the kind robber can't walk you home. Home is beyond all three. And the first step is noticing: the moment you can say, oh, that's rajas, you're already a little outside it.
screen: `ONE RISES, TWO FALL.` · `LIGHT, GREED, OR FOG.` · `KNOWLEDGE, GREED, CONFUSION.` · `SATTVA SHOWS THE ROAD.` · then, large: `HOME IS BEYOND THE THREE.`

segments.voice: Scan yourself for the Gita's field marks. Light and clear seeing, through the eyes and ears: the bright thread. Restlessness, wanting, an itch in the hands to start something new: the moving thread. Fog, heaviness, a wish to go blank: the heavy one. Whatever is strongest, name it softly, the way Nani might: ah, that's rajas. Then rest as the one who noticed. The robbers move; the watcher isn't one of them.
Rajas, passion, motion, heat: the robber who ties you up. Gita fourteen, twelve: its marks are greed, busyness, starting one thing after another, restlessness and longing.
Your line: tamas strikes, rajas binds, sattva shows the road. Home is beyond all three. Two hundred eight days now.

209.title: Beyond the three gunas
209.hook: Arjuna asks what a person beyond the three threads looks like
209.carry: beyond the three gunas, through devotion
209.howItsDone: Hindu teachers hold up the gunatita of Gita 14.22–14.25 as a picture of spiritual maturity; many devotional traditions point to 14.26, unwavering devotion, as the way there.

segments.voice: Yesterday: tamas strikes, rajas binds, sattva shows the road, and the traveler still isn't home. Today, Arjuna asks what the one who gets home looks like.
screen: `TAMAS STRIKES, RAJAS BINDS, SATTVA SHOWS THE ROAD.`

segments.voice: Post something online and watch what happens to you. A hundred likes, and you feel tall. One cruel comment, and it rattles around your head all night. The hundred don't cancel out the one. Plenty of people are built this way: praise lifts, blame drops, and managing both takes a lot of energy. At the end of chapter fourteen, Arjuna asks a very practical question. What does someone look like who has gone beyond the three threads? How do they act? How do they get there?
screen: `A HUNDRED LIKES.` → `ONE CRUEL COMMENT.` → `WHO ISN'T MOVED BY EITHER?`

segments.voice: Arjuna's question is verse twenty-one, and it has three parts: the marks, the behavior, the way. Krishna answers with a portrait. Verse twenty-two: when light, activity and confusion come, this person doesn't hate them; when they go, doesn't long for them. The threads still show up. Even the person beyond the gunas has sleepy mornings and busy afternoons. The difference is the grip. Verse twenty-three: they sit like someone unconcerned, udasina, literally sitting above, not shaken by the gunas, knowing it's just the threads moving. Verse twenty-four: the same in sorrow and happiness, resting in the self; a lump of clay, a stone and gold are all the same to them. The same toward the pleasant and the unpleasant, steady, the same in blame and in praise of themselves. Verse twenty-five: the same in honor and dishonor, the same to friend and enemy. That person, Krishna says, has gone beyond the gunas. Gunatita. Then the answer to the third question, how to get there. Verse twenty-six: the one who serves me with unwavering devotion goes beyond the three and becomes fit for Brahman. So the way beyond isn't a technique for crushing the threads. In this chapter, it's bhakti, love. Verse twenty-seven closes: I am the ground of Brahman, of the deathless, of lasting dharma, and of perfect joy. This isn't indifference. It's the steadiness of someone whose center is somewhere the likes and comments can't reach.
screen: `THE THREADS STILL COME AND GO.` · `SITTING ABOVE, UNSHAKEN.` · `CLAY, STONE AND GOLD, THE SAME.` · `THE WAY BEYOND IS DEVOTION.` · then, large: `BEYOND THE THREE.`

segments.voice: Remember a recent word of praise and let it land; notice the lift in the chest. Then a recent word of blame, and notice the drop. If you pray, offer both to God, the way verse twenty-six points. If you don't, simply sit a little above both, like someone watching weather from a hill: the lift and the drop still come; you're just not living inside them.
Gunatita, gone beyond the gunas. Gita fourteen: the one who has gone beyond the gunas doesn't hate them when they come or long for them when they go, and is the same in praise and blame.
Your line: beyond the three gunas, through devotion. The threads still come; love loosens their grip. Until tomorrow.

210.title: The tree with roots above
210.hook: chapter fifteen opens with a sacred fig tree growing upside down
210.carry: the world is a tree rooted in God
210.howItsDone: The peepal (ashvattha, sacred fig) is honored by Hindus: some water it, tie threads around it and walk around it; Gita 15 uses it as an image of the world, and some recite chapter fifteen on its own.

segments.voice: Yesterday: beyond the three gunas, through devotion; the threads still come, but they lose their grip. Now, a tree.

A huge old peepal tree stands at the edge of a village square. Threads are tied around its trunk. Someone walks slow circles around it. Two old men sit in its shade and argue about cricket. Its heart-shaped leaves tremble in the slightest breeze. It's the sacred fig, the ashvattha. Now flip that tree over in your mind: roots up in the sky, branches hanging down, spreading all over the earth. That strange picture is how chapter fifteen begins.
screen: `THE OLD PEEPAL IN THE VILLAGE.` → `THREADS TIED AROUND ITS TRUNK.` → `NOW FLIP IT OVER.`

segments.voice: Verse one. They speak of an undying ashvattha tree with its roots above and its branches below. Its leaves are the Vedic hymns. Whoever knows this tree knows the Vedas. Back in chapter ten, Krishna said that among trees he is the ashvattha, and many Hindus point to that line when they honor the peepal. So what's the tree? Commentators read it as the whole world of change, samsara, the round of birth and death. Its roots are above because it grows from the highest source. Verse two: its branches spread up and down, fed by the three gunas, and its buds are the objects of the senses. Some roots stretch downward too, into the human world, tangling us in action. That's why the tree feels so real: we're hanging in its branches, and the branches keep growing. Verse three is honest: its real shape can't be seen from here, not its end, not its beginning, not what it stands on. Then the surprise. This huge, deep-rooted tree, Krishna says, cut it down with the strong axe of non-attachment. Asanga, not clinging. Not with violence, not by running away, but by letting go. Verse four: then seek that place from which no one returns, and take refuge in the first person, from whom this ancient flow came. Verse six says that place isn't lit by sun, moon or fire. It's my highest home. This stretch ran through the field, humility, the one light, the three threads, how they show up, and going beyond them. Today it all becomes one picture.
screen: `ROOTS ABOVE, BRANCHES BELOW.` · `THE LEAVES ARE HYMNS.` · `THE AXE OF NOT CLINGING.` · `A HOME NO SUN LIGHTS.` · then, large: `THE TREE WITH ROOTS ABOVE.`

segments.voice: Picture yourself among the branches of a great tree, each branch something you hold on to: a plan, a worry, a person, a wish. Feel your grip on one, and without dropping anything, loosen it a little; that's the axe the Gita means, not clinging. Then let your attention travel up the trunk toward the roots, the source, and rest there.
Ashvattha, the sacred fig. Gita fifteen: the world of change as an upside-down tree, rooted in the highest, cut with the axe of not clinging.
Your line: the world is a tree rooted in God. Roots in the highest, branches in our lives. Day two hundred ten, complete.
